title: Complete persuasion vs the minimum without which true faith cannot stand
source_text: XVII. Adde quod alii fidem justificantem describunt secundum esse suum completum & perfectum, & secundum id quod ex se apta nata est in fideli producere. Ut qui illi tribuunt firmam & certam persuasionem quod fidelis sit in Dei gratia, & quod peccata illi remissa sint, absque quo tamen fides in fideli infirmo, saltem ad tempus, potest subsistere: alii vero fidem definiunt ex iis sine quibus vera fides, quantumlibet parva & debilis, ne ad minimum quidem constare potest. Ut qui illam definiunt per famem & sitim justitiae, & cordis in Deo acquiescentiam. Quae postea distinctius & clarius intelligentur, quum sigillatim explicuerimus varios fidei actus, secundum Scholae Reformatae Doctores.
pass_a_gloss: Add that some describe justifying faith according to its complete and perfect being, and according to what it is by nature apt to produce in the faithful. As those who attribute to it a firm and sure persuasion that the faithful is in God's grace, and that sins have been remitted to him — without which nevertheless faith can subsist in a weak believer, at least for a time: but others define faith from those things without which true faith, however small and weak, cannot stand even minimally. As those who define it through hunger and thirst for justice, and the heart's resting in God. Which afterward will be understood more distinctly and clearly, when we shall have explained one by one the various acts of faith, according to the Doctors of the Reformed School.
pass_b_english: Some define justifying faith by its complete/perfect state — firm sure persuasion of being in grace and of remitted sins.
Yet weak faith can subsist for a time without that full persuasion.
Others define by the minimum without which true faith — however small — cannot stand.
Hunger and thirst for justice; heart's rest in God. Acts of faith come next.
